entities.name: Cleitus the Illyrian
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cleitus the Illyrian, a king of the Illyrian tribe of the Dardani or possibly the Taulantii, emerged as a formidable opponent to Alexander III of Macedon during his early reign in 335 BCE. His significance lies in leading one of the most serious and widespread rebellions against Macedonian authority on Alexander's European frontier, demanding Alexander's personal attention and demonstrating the persistent desire for independence among Balkan tribes against the burgeoning Hellenistic empire. Alongside Glaucias, king of the Taulantii, Cleitus represented a crucial challenge to the stability of Alexander's newly inherited kingdom before his grand campaign into Asia.

The core events of Cleitus's resistance unfolded in 335 BCE. While Alexander was campaigning against the Triballi and Getae to the north, Cleitus took advantage of the opportunity to revolt. He captured the strategically vital city of Pelium (likely modern Selcë e Poshtme, Albania) and allied with Glaucias, blocking the Eordaic Pass. Alexander, upon learning of the rebellion, swiftly marched his forces to relieve Pelium. The ensuing siege was a complex affair, involving tactical maneuvers by both sides, including Alexander's famous feigned retreat and subsequent surprise attack, which ultimately led to the Illyrian forces abandoning Pelium and fleeing into the Taulantian mountains after burning the city.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cleitus the Illyrian's rebellion was one of the most significant challenges to Alexander the Great's early reign, forcing Alexander to personally secure his European frontier before embarking on his conquest of Asia. His defeat directly led to the consolidation of Macedonian power in the Balkans for decades.
